issues.legal_issue: A reviewing custodian may revise a subordinate property order only after giving the affected person a reasonable opportunity to be heard, but a formal or separately worded notice is unnecessary when the person understands the scope of the review and is heard.
material_facts: In one appeal, the custodian reviewed matters not included in the appeal from the subordinate officer’s order, and the affected person’s counsel was informed that those matters might be revised and was heard on them.

In the other appeal, the notice did not refer specifically to the dissolution deed, but the affected person’s response showed that he understood that the related settlement statements and transaction were under review, and his advocate was heard.
issues.conclusion: The reviewing custodian acted in revisional jurisdiction, and the absence of a formal or specifically worded notice did not invalidate either order because the affected person had a reasonable opportunity to be heard.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 26(1) of the Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950, a person must receive a reasonable opportunity to be heard before a prejudicial revisional order is made. The section does not specifically require service of a formal notice; notice is necessary when it is needed to provide that opportunity, but its omission is immaterial where the person is already before the custodian, understands the matter under review, and is heard. The Court relied on no earlier cases for this principle.

predicates.revision_of_subordinate_property_order: A reviewing authority examined whether to revise an order made by a subordinate property authority.
predicates.affected_party_understood_review_scope: The affected person knew which order or transaction the reviewing authority was considering revising.
predicates.affected_party_was_heard: The affected person or their representative was given an opportunity to present arguments before the reviewing authority.

issues.definition: When a subordinate property order is under review, an affected person who understands the scope of that review and is heard cannot have the resulting order invalidated solely because formal or specifically worded notice was omitted.

issues.legal_issue: Dissolution of a partnership does not by itself transfer an evacuee partner’s interest to the other partner, and a declaration concerning the dissolved business may identify the property remaining in the evacuee’s interest on dissolution.
material_facts: The business was conducted by two partners, one of whom was accepted to be an evacuee.

The dissolution deed was executed on a later date than the date of dissolution it recited; the custodian rejected the asserted earlier date, and the Court accepted the deed’s execution date as the date of dissolution.
The properties in question were assets of the partnership, and the deed of dissolution did not by itself transfer the evacuee partner’s share to the other partner.
issues.conclusion: The declaration concerning the business was properly understood as applying to the property remaining in the evacuee partner’s interest when the partnership was dissolved; dissolution alone did not transfer that interest to the other partner.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied the principle that dissolution does not itself transfer one partner’s share to another. It construed the declaration concerning the business as concerning the property remaining in the evacuee’s interest on dissolution. The Court also treated the deed’s execution date, rather than its recited earlier date, as the date of dissolution on the findings before it. No earlier cases were relied on for this issue.

predicates.evacuee_partnership_interest: A person who is an evacuee holds an interest in a partnership and its assets.
predicates.property_remained_in_evacuee_interest: An interest in partnership property remained attributable to the evacuee when the partnership was dissolved.

issues.definition: If a dissolved partnership leaves property attributable to an evacuee partner, that remaining interest may be treated as evacuee property, and dissolution alone does not transfer it to another partner.

issues.legal_issue: A transfer of an evacuee’s partnership interest made without good faith has no effect against the evacuee estate, and the custodian is not bound by the deed’s stated settlement of partnership accounts.
material_facts: The sale and dissolution deeds purported to transfer or settle the evacuee partner’s interests in partnership assets.
The custodian found the transactions not bona fide, and the Court upheld that finding.
The sale deed was executed before the actual dissolution, so it could not be treated as a step in winding up the dissolved partnership.
The custodian’s declaration concerned the evacuee’s share in the dissolved partnership, and the partnership accounts had not been settled independently of the statements in the deed.
issues.conclusion: The purported transfer of the evacuee’s interest had no effect; the custodian was not bound by the deed’s account-settlement statements and held the rights the evacuee had under partnership law in relation to the dissolved business.
issues.legal_principle: Section 40 of the Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950, makes a transfer by an evacuee without good faith of no effect. The custodian in whom the evacuee property vests has the evacuee’s relevant rights under sections 37, 46, 47 and 48, and other applicable provisions, of the Indian Partnership Act, 1932; the custodian is not bound by settlement statements in the dissolution deed. The Court relied on no earlier cases for this issue.

predicates.proceeding_concerns_evacuee_property: The proceeding concerns property or an interest attributable to an evacuee.
predicates.transfer_of_evacuee_partnership_interest: A deed or other transaction purports to transfer an evacuee’s interest in partnership property.
predicates.transfer_was_not_bona_fide: The purported transfer was found not to have been made in good faith.

issues.definition: A purported transfer of an evacuee’s partnership interest in a proceeding concerning evacuee property has no effect against the evacuee estate when the transfer was not made in good faith.

issues.legal_issue: When the governing definition treats evacuee property as property of the evacuee, only the evacuee’s share in jointly held partnership property is evacuee property, not the entire property.
material_facts: The properties at issue were assets of a partnership in which the evacuee and the other partner each held an equal share.
The custodian’s order referred to the entire scheduled properties, although its conclusion identified the evacuee’s eight-anna share.
The statutory definition had been amended to refer to property of an evacuee rather than property in which an evacuee had any right or interest.
issues.conclusion: Only the evacuee’s eight-anna share in the scheduled properties was to be treated as evacuee property, not the entire properties.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 2(f) of the Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950, as amended, evacuee property means property of an evacuee. The Court distinguished this from the former wording, which covered property in which an evacuee had any right or interest, and clarified that only the evacuee’s share was within the amended definition. No earlier cases were relied on for this issue.

predicates.proceeding_classifies_jointly_held_prope: A proceeding determines whether jointly held property is evacuee property.
predicates.evacuee_owns_only_a_share: The evacuee holds less than the whole interest in the jointly held property.

issues.definition: When a classification proceeding concerns jointly held property and the evacuee owns only a share, only that share is treated as evacuee property.
